What the Fog Left Audible

[1] On the first morning of the survey, fog erased the reeds across the narrow channel. [2] I had volunteered to help count birds in a restored marsh. [3] I believed I was prepared because I had studied photographs in a field guide.[1] With my binoculars raised, I waited for the gray air to clear.

Noor, the survey leader, suggested that I lower the binoculars and listen. At first, the marsh seemed to manufacture[2] one continuous rustle. Then Noor separated it into parts, a dry rattle came from the reeds, and three clear whistles sounded from a willow.[3] She named each bird only after repeating the pattern back to me.

Each observer carried a clipboard divided into five-minute intervals. The observers marked every bird he[4] detected and noted whether the identification came from sight or sound. Noor warned me not to count a call that I could not distinguish confidently. Consequently,[5] certainty mattered more than filling every blank on the page.

[A] We followed the boardwalk toward a stand of cattails. [B] Noor asked me to describe a call before trying to name its source.[6] I heard two low notes, a pause, and a faster series of clicks. [C] She repeated my description and pointed out that the pause stayed nearly constant. [D] A sequence of calls from the cattails were[7] enough for us to record one marsh wren without seeing it.

During the next interval, I recognized the same rhythm farther along the boardwalk. I checked its spacing twice before quietly reporting it. Noor nodded and entered the observation. I did not feel that I had become the greatest bird expert the marsh had ever known.[8] Instead, I felt useful because I could explain what I had heard and why I trusted it. By the time the fog lifted, I identified[9] four birds by sound and two by sight.

Sunlight eventually returned color and distance to the marsh, but I did not raise my binoculars as quickly as before. The fog had not hidden the birds so much as exposed my narrow way of looking for them. Since that morning, listening has not replaced seeing; it has made every survey a fuller act of attention.[10]
